items.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter addresses that analytical fragmentation by developing a comparative framework through which localization rules, AI governance instruments, and sovereignty claims are examined as mutually conditioning layers of digital statecraft rather than as isolated legal categories. A structured review of an uploaded Scopus corpus, which contained 139 records, was combined with a comparative analysis of India, Indonesia, Kenya, and Brazil, alongside official instruments issued by the African Union, UNESCO, the OECD, and NIST. The analysis demonstrates that broad territorial restrictions on data do not by themselves produce operational digital sovereignty; durable sovereignty is achieved when selective localization is aligned with data classification, compute and cloud capacity, risk-based AI governance, and interoperable cross-border transfer mechanisms.</jats:p>
title: Data Localization, AI Governance, and Digital Sovereignty in Emerging Economies

items.abstract: <jats:p>The exponential growth of data has turned transnational data governance into a strategic priority for global data hubs. While the concept of “data as the new oil” highlights big data’s economic value, the dominance of large technology firms and increasing geopolitical tensions have prompted states, particularly China, to assert stronger control over cross‐border data flows. Since the 2016 Cybersecurity Law, China’s legislative approach has evolved significantly, culminating in comprehensive frameworks such as the Personal Information Protection Law and the Data Security Law. While prior research has focused on China’s legal infrastructure and data localization mandates, this study examines the adaptive and geopolitical dimensions of its transnational data governance strategy—an area that remains underexplored. Drawing on a content analysis of central‐level legislation from 2016 to 2024, this study identifies shifting legislative priorities, governance mechanisms, and legal rationales. The findings show that China has developed a multi‐layered and increasingly flexible legal regime that balances sovereignty claims with selective openness, reflecting a pragmatic response to domestic needs and international pressures. This study expands the original scope of the “Beijing effect” by showing that China’s influence on global data governance extends beyond the export of digital infrastructure to include dynamic legal adaptation and strategic regulatory innovation.</jats:p>
title: Adaptive Sovereignty: China’s Evolving Legislative Framework for Transnational Data Governance

items.abstract: <jats:p>Over time, data has replaced oil as the central resource around which narratives of African development revolve., and yet the leading data-generating economies in Africa have remarkably little control over where such data will reside, by whom it will be processed and under what legal terms and conditions it may leave national territory. Nigeria, Africa's largest digital market by user base, illustrates this paradox acutely: a domestic data protection statute of considerable technical sophistication sits atop an infrastructure landscape still overwhelmingly dependent on foreign-owned cloud platforms, undersea cables, and hyperscale data centres. This paper probes the notion of data sovereignty for the Nigerian digital economy, theoretically distinguishes it from conceptually cognate (yet not coterminous) data localisation, data protection, and digital sovereignty. It provides a critique of the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and the earlier regulation governing cross border data transfer within the EU's GDPR; India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023; and China's framework on data security; analyzes the supranational regulatory space constituted by the Malabo Convention, the AU Data Policy Framework, and the recently adopted AfCFTA Protocol on digital Trade; argues that Nigeria’s failure to ratify the Malabo Convention reflects a larger lack of intra-continental consensus for collective bargaining with global technology companies. The paper ultimately argues that data sovereignty, properly conceived, is neither an act of digital autarky nor exclusively a claim of territorial dominion over the digital realm, rather, it represents an essential project of institution building: Nigeria lacks neither the technical or legal capacity for the regime but that it requires-institutionally credible regulators; selectively targeted localisation of strategically important categories of data; and active cooperation with other African Union states toward common legal frameworks-rather than a maximalist embrace of territoriality that risks economic disadvantage. It concludes with targeted recommendations for the NDPA; the National Assembly and AU bodies.</jats:p>
title: <p>Data Sovereignty in Africa: Building A Sustainable Framework for Cross-Border Data Governance in Nigeria's Digital Economy</p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Digital sovereignty has become a central objective in European public-sector digital policy, driven by increasing dependence on foreign cloud service providers, heightened geopolitical uncertainty, and the strategic importance of data-driven government functions. The dominant policy response has been the pursuit of sovereign cloud strategies, which seek to reconcile cloud adoption with sovereignty through jurisdictional alignment, compliance frameworks, and certification schemes. This paper argues that such infrastructure-centric approaches misidentify the primary object of sovereignty and therefore struggle to deliver effective and verifiable control. It contributes a reframing of digital sovereignty by relocating sovereignty from cloud infrastructure and jurisdictional alignment to enforceable, verifiable data control as the primary locus of authority. Drawing on literature from digital governance, platform economics, and public-sector cloud policy, this paper introduces data-centric sovereignty as an alternative conceptual framework. Data-centric sovereignty defines sovereignty as exclusive and enforceable control over data-encompassing access, availability, cryptographic key custody, and decision authority-independent of the underlying cloud or any infrastructure. <jats:p><div>
 The rapid development of artificial intelligence, neurotechnologies, and cognitive augmentation systems is progressively transforming the relationship between human cognition and technological infrastructures. This transformation raises fundamental questions regarding the preservation of human autonomy, intellectual freedom, and decision-making sovereignty in environments increasingly influenced by algorithmic systems.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 This article introduces the HUMROBOT analytical framework, a conceptual and systemic model designed to examine the evolution of the interaction between human cognition and intelligent technological systems. Building on previous work that introduced the concept of cognitive sovereignty, the present study proposes a structured model for analyzing the dynamics of hybridization between humans and technology as well as their implications for governance, ethics, and human autonomy.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 The HUMROBOT framework conceptualizes the human-technology relationship as a dynamic system structured around three fundamental forces: technology, human cognition, and governance. The model also introduces a typology of hybrid cognitive conditions and proposes a governance structure aimed at preserving cognitive sovereignty while enabling responsible technological innovation.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 By integrating contributions from the philosophy of technology, cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence ethics, and governance theory, this work aims to contribute to contemporary debates concerning the future of human autonomy in technologically augmented environments.
</div></jats:p>
title: Analytical Framework and Governance of Cognitive Sovereignty in Human-Machine Hybridization

<jats:p>Abstract:
This book explores the intricate frameworks, tensions, and solutions at the intersection of artificial intelligence governance, data sovereignty, cybersecurity, and ethical compliance. It provides a globally comparative and multidisciplinary analysis of how public and private entities are navigating rapidly evolving AI environments. Examining regulatory models, data localization laws, algorithmic transparency, AI ethics, cyber defense, and sector-specific risks, the book offers an actionable roadmap for governments, corporations, and civil society to ensure responsible and sovereign AI adoption. It advocates for adaptive policy architectures, interoperable compliance standards, and inclusive governance mechanisms that balance innovation with public interest.

Keywords: AI governance, data sovereignty, cybersecurity, ethical AI, compliance, regulation, algorithmic bias, digital sovereignty, transparency, accountability</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of algorithmic systems into critical digital infrastructure is no longer peripheral to governance, it is governance. As AI-mediated decisions influence credit access, clinical diagnoses, criminal risk scores, and infrastructure routing, the question of who controls these algorithms and whether that control is meaningful has become a central concern for states and institutions at every level of development. Existing frameworks, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act, have made real progress toward structured AI governance. However, none treats digital sovereignty as a first-order goal, nor do they provide integrated cross-layer guidance applicable across the diverse institutional landscape found worldwide. From this synthesis, we develop the Integrated AI Risk Governance Framework (IARGF): a four-layer structure covering policy and regulations, institutional oversight, technical controls, and operational execution, organized around five risk categories—technical, ethical, security, systemic, and sovereignty-related. A comparative analysis with major existing frameworks highlights the IARGF’s unique contributions, especially its explicit focus on sovereignty, adaptability across different institutional capacities, and recursive feedback mechanisms that connect all four governance layers. The framework is analyzed across three domains—healthcare AI, financial services, and critical infrastructure—to demonstrate its practical utility. Results confirm that governance effectiveness is a system property, not just a feature of individual layers; that digital sovereignty is both a governance goal and a distinct risk dimension with specific technical and institutional needs; and that context-aware, capacity-scaled governance is a design requirement, not a political compromise. The IARGF is presented as a conceptual governance model based on a systematic literature review rather than an empirically validated tool, and it remains to be tested in actual organizational settings. Its main contribution is the comprehensive theoretical integration of sovereignty, institutional capacity, and inter-layer governance dynamics, rather than proven performance advantages over existing models. Future research should aim to validate this framework through longitudinal case studies, expert panels, and retrospective failure analyses.</jats:p>
title: AI Risk Governance for Advancing Digital Sovereignty in Data-Driven Systems: An Integrated Multi-Layer Framework

<jats:p>Canada is at a strategic inflection point. Its digital sovereignty depends directly on three inseparable levers: data interoperability across federal, provincial and territorial (FPT) governments; sovereign cloud infrastructure; and the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector. These levers form an integrated architecture that drives productivity, digital security, government modernization and the country’s capacity to address the current fragmentation of public information systems.

Analysis of the 2025 federal budget confirms an ambitious repositioning around productivity, economic sovereignty, infrastructure resilience and digital transformation. However, in the absence of an explicit FPT framework for data interoperability, investments remain dispersed and struggle to produce systemic effects.
Canada nonetheless has structural advantages: a tradition of intergovernmental collaboration an internationally respected national statistical system and a proven ability to build shared governance mechanisms. Today’s fragmentation, spread across fourteen heterogeneous digital infrastructures with divergent standards, metadata and identifiers, directly undermines public-sector efficiency, critical-infrastructure security and the responsible use of AI.

The CIRANO Burgundy Report (CIRANO, 2025) underscores that the Canadian federation has the conceptual foundations to build federated data governance, provided the legislative framework is modernized (including an update to Bill C-27), institutional responsibilities are clarified, and mutualization of resources approaches are strengthened.
International comparisons, particularly with the European Union, show that jurisdictions that have successfully advanced digital transformation rely on robust interoperability architectures, common repositories, standardized trust frameworks and mechanisms for pooling digital capabilities.


Technical considerations demonstrate concretely what is required: harmonized metadata, common identifiers, secure sharing mechanisms, sovereign cloud infrastructures and compatible modular services. Recent steps—the creation of the Office of Digital Transformation (ODT), investments announced in Budget 2025 and the emerging vision for a sovereign cloud, are significant but insufficient without a structured FPT framework for public-sector data interoperability and AI adoption.

This analysis highlights that data interoperability must be recognized as essential infrastructure, on par with energy networks and transportation corridors. It is indispensable for consistent public services, lower transaction costs, stronger privacy protection, crisis resilience and value creation through AI. The identification of high-value FPT data, risk management, digital operational sovereignty and the role of shared entities reinforce the need for a permanent FPT Board on data interoperability and AI.

By harmonizing standards, investments and institutional capacities, FPT governments can transform current digital fragmentation into a driver of cohesion, productivity, sovereignty and public innovation. FPT interoperability and responsible AI are not technical add-ons; they are the foundations of a strong, sustainable and truly sovereign Canadian digital economy.</jats:p>
title: Digital Sovereignty and federalism: Data Interoperability and AI governance

items.abstract: <jats:p>Transnational education (TNE), defined as higher education provision in which learners are located in a country other than that awarding the credential, has undergone a structural transformation from physically bounded delivery modalities toward digitally mediated cross-border systems. This paper examines the structural opportunities, systemic tensions, and governance challenges that characterise contemporary digital TNE. Drawing on a critical conceptual analysis of interdisciplinary literature covering the period from 2007 to 2025, the paper investigates three interrelated problem domains: the conditions under which digital delivery extends access to historically marginalised populations; the regulatory fragmentation and data governance asymmetries that impede institutional accountability; and the epistemological consequences of a global digital education architecture concentrated within Western academic institutions and technology firms. Engaging the theoretical frameworks of Santos (2014), Mignolo (2009, 2011), Ndlovu-Gatsheni (2018), and Spivak (1988), the paper argues that access, taken alone, is an insufficient measure of equity when the underlying knowledge architectures reproduce colonial epistemological hierarchies. The paper contributes an original three-layer co-governance framework that integrates regulatory harmonisation, low-resource infrastructure design, and pluriversal curriculum coproduction as a coherent response to the structural deficiencies of current digital TNE arrangements. The framework is offered as a conceptual instrument for policymakers, institutional leaders, and accreditation bodies engaged in reforming cross-border higher education governance.</jats:p>
title: Digital Transnational Education, Epistemic Sovereignty, and the Governance of Knowledge: A Critical Analytical Framework

items.abstract: <jats:p>The EU has explicitly linked the concept of data sovereignty to its ambitions as an international regulatory agenda‐setter in its position as self‐described geopolitical union. In particular, the EU has expressed repeatedly its desire to ensure its strategic autonomy, reducing its dependence on third countries and their key industries. The purpose of this article is to explore EU data governance ambitions by highlighting the gap between those autonomy aspirations and the reality of data interdependence on the ground. More specifically, through the framework of the “autonomy‐interdependence” governance gap, the article proposes to analyse the clash between the EU’s desire to ensure autonomy and the inherently interdependent nature of data flows between states, and its dependence on non‐EU data servers. Using the case study of semiconductor supply chains, this article analyses the data dimension of this EU‐designated critical technology, and the flows of information relating to the research, design, and fabrication of these chips. Considering the EU’s attempts to control data under its Data Act and Data Governance Act, it argues that the EU will have considerable difficulty in operationalising these data sovereignty ambitions, particularly as they relate to ensuring that all data stays within the EU, or within its sphere of regulatory influence.</jats:p>
title: EU Data Sovereignty: An Autonomy–Interdependence Governance Gap?

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems in healthcare operate in high-stakes environments where algorithmic decisions directly affect patient outcomes, privacy, and autonomy. This paper introduces the Five Ways Framework, a comprehensive ethical architecture integrating five interconnected pillars: core ethical principles, blockchain transparency, autonomous AI agent oversight, data governance, and self-sovereign digital identity. The framework addresses the critical challenge of protecting patient privacy and sovereignty while enabling the transformative potential of AI-driven healthcare. We validate the framework using the MIMIC-IV dataset, demonstrating measurable improvements in privacy protection (k-anonymity ≥ 5), algorithmic fairness (bias metrics < 0.1), consent compliance (> 95%), and audit trail completeness (100%). Our findings indicate that ethical design strengthens both technical outcomes and stakeholder confidence.
title: The Five Ways Framework for AI Ethics in Healthcare: Integrating Core Ethical Principles, Blockchain Transparency, Autonomous Agents, Data Governance, and Digital Identity for Patient Privacy and Sovereignty

items.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the challenges of governing cross-border data flows within a fragmented global legal landscape with a focus on the tension between digital sovereignty and transnational data mobility. It argues that legal fragmentation is a structural feature of contemporary data governance, producing regulatory conflicts and reinforcing power asymmetries between states, corporations and individuals. The chapter analyses how state-led sovereignty strategies and societal as well as technological resistance seek to address these challenges but often reproduce underlying fragmentation. It then explores pathways toward more coherent governance through interoperability, institutional coordination and shared normative principles. In doing so, it highlights the importance of aligning global data governance with broader commitments to inclusive development, accountability and the values reflected in the sustainable development goals.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>This chapter describes a shift from territorial to functional sovereignty online, as private firms increasingly assume the prerogatives of governance. It interprets a series of trends in the United States as assertions of firms’ functional sovereignty over the platforms and services they operate, which in turn rule relations among their users with little to no state interference. This shift from territorial to functional sovereignty is creating a new digital political economy, particularly where governments find themselves increasingly dependent on technology firms for vital infrastructure. The article concludes with reflections on the comparative desirability of functional and territorial sovereignty. The erosion of states’ sovereignty over online life may not disperse power, but instead concentrate it in less accountable actors.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The accelerating digital transformation of healthcare in Africa presents both a remarkable opportunity and a profound governance challenge. Across the continent, countries are adopting electronic health records, mobile platforms, and disease surveillance tools that promise to improve service delivery, expand access, and strengthen health equity. Yet these gains remain uneven and fragile because of fragmented governance structures, siloed donor-driven platforms, and limited use of real-time analytics for public health decision-making. Equally pressing is the ethical gap in consent practices, where Western-inspired one-time models fail to reflect Africa’s communal values, linguistic diversity, and varying levels of digital literacy. These issues weaken trust and constrain the continent’s ability to achieve true health data sovereignty. This article introduces the Integrated Data Sovereignty Framework (IDSF), a conceptual model that unites three interdependent pillars: centralized data governance, real-time analytics, and ethically anchored user rights and consent. The article demonstrates how interoperable data hubs, mobile technologies, and culturally grounded electronic consent mechanisms can enhance responsiveness while preserving sovereignty by drawing on African case examples from Ghana, Rwanda, Nigeria, Liberia, and South Africa. The framework is informed by institutional theory, sociotechnical systems thinking, collective benefits, authority to control, responsibility, and ethics, which are referred to as CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance, ensuring that it is theoretically robust and contextually grounded. By synthesizing these insights, the article positions the Integrated Data Sovereignty Framework as a strategic response to Africa’s evolving digital health landscape. It highlights pathways for low- and middle-income countries to move beyond fragmented donor-led models toward sovereign, resilient, and trusted data ecosystems. The study concludes with policy recommendations for national reforms, pilot testing of dynamic consent and analytics platforms, and cross-border data collaborations under African Union and Africa CDC initiatives. Ultimately, it argues that digital health sovereignty is not simply technical; it is a moral and political imperative for building equitable, transparent, and sustainable healthcare systems in Africa.</jats:p>
title: Building Trust and Sovereignty: A Holistic Framework for Data Governance in African Healthcare Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>The proliferation of privately operated Low Earth Orbit ("LEO") communications satellites has dramatically changed the way governments around the globe manage their national communication networks. Satellite-based internet services, such as SpaceX&apos;s Starlink, have the potential to greatly enhance digital access in rural and underserved areas of India with limited or no terrestrial infrastructure. On the other hand, increased reliance on foreign-controlled orbital communication infrastructure raises significant issues regarding sovereignty over communications, cybersecurity governance, strategic autonomy, lawful interception, data protection, and regulatory oversight. In contrast to land-based telecommunications systems that rely on territory-based infrastructure (e.g., towers), decentralised satellite communication systems utilise global distribution networks, which significantly complicate prior assumptions about territorial jurisdiction and central government oversight. This research will argue that India&apos;s current telecommunications or satellite communications regulations remain primarily grounded in a territorial regulatory paradigm and therefore lack an institutional foundation to regulate foreign-controlled or artificially-intelligent orbital communication ecosystems. This article also explores the integration of artificial intelligence ("AI") technologies into satellite communication systems, utilising automation of satellite system operations, including network coordination, cybersecurity surveillance and predictive maintenance, as well as AI-enabled management of satellite infrastructure. Utilising a doctrinal and comparative techno-regulatory approach, it analyses India&apos;s emerging regulatory environment against the backdrop of regulatory developments in Europe (EU), China, and the U.S. It utilises the term "Orbital Sovereignty" to advocate for greater synergy among the various aspects of strategic infrastructural governance.</jats:p>
title: Orbital Sovereignty and AI-Enabled Security Risks: Reimagining India’s Satellite Communication Governance Framework

items.abstract: <jats:p>This case study examines the constitutional, regulatory and operational difficulties that have attended Kenya’s three successive attempts to deploy a national digital identity system: the Huduma Namba (2019), the Huduma Card (2021) and the Maisha Namba (2023 to present). Each generation has been challenged in the High Court, and in each case the same legal flaw has been determinative: the state proceeded with population-scale processing of personal data without first conducting a data protection impact assessment under section 31 of the Data Protection Act, No. 24 of 2019. The case asks how a state should respond when its preferred operational path has been twice declared unlawful, and a third generation of the same system is now before the courts.</jats:p>
title: Kenya: Huduma or Hegemony? Digital Identity, Data Sovereignty and the Governance Gap

items.abstract: <jats:p>Malaysia's digital transformation has intensified the datafication of migrant labour through biometric registration, immigration databases, recruitment platforms, health surveillance systems, employer-linked portals, and algorithmic workplace monitoring. However, dominant debates on data sovereignty often remain state-centric, focusing on territorial control, national security, infrastructure, and cross-border data flows while paying limited attention to noncitizen workers whose bodies, mobility, labour, and legal status are increasingly governed through digital systems. This working paper argues that migrant workers in Malaysia face a specific form of digital vulnerability produced by the intersection of visa dependency, employer power, platform surveillance, weak regulatory protection, and crossborder data circulation. Drawing on critical data studies, migration governance, data colonialism, and Chowdhury's work on reciprocity, Indigenous Gnoseology, Ubuntu, and migrant worker voice, the paper proposes a shift from state-centric data sovereignty to relational data justice. Relational data justice recognizes migrant workers not as passive data objects but as rights-bearing subjects with legitimate claims to access, correction, consent, explanation, redress, and collective participation in data governance. The paper develops three principles: worker-centred authority over data, reciprocal accountability of data-collecting institutions, and collective protection against algorithmic and biometric harm. It concludes that ethical digital governance in Malaysia and ASEAN must begin from the dignity, agency, and lived vulnerability of migrant workers.</jats:p>
title: From Data Sovereignty to Data Justice: Migrant Workers, Digital Governance, and Relational Rights in Malaysia

                  <jats:p>This article presents the development of a five‐phase Indigenous Data Governance (IDGov) Framework in Australia, focusing on partnerships between the Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (ACCHO) sector and non‐Indigenous health entities. While the Indigenous Data Sovereignty (IDSov) movement has gained significant momentum over the past decade in Australia and other Anglo‐colonised nation‐states and beyond, the practical implementation of IDSov through community‐led governance remains underdeveloped in the literature. This paper addresses that gap by offering definitional and conceptual clarity, alongside examples that center Indigenous leadership in operationalising data governance. We introduce a phased model of IDGov, mapping a progression from the absence of governance through partial and shared arrangements to Indigenous‐majority and fully Indigenous‐led governance structures. The model is illustrated through a case study involving a complex data‐sharing agreement between one Indigenous and three non‐Indigenous organisations within the Victorian health system. Roles and responsibilities across each phase are articulated to support practical implementation. While grounded in the health sector, the framework is adaptable to other domains such as education, justice, and land governance, where IDSov is increasingly critical. This work offers a pathway for operationalising IDSov and transforming data relations to reflect and uphold Indigenous rights, worldviews, and decision‐making authority.</jats:p>
title: Implementing Indigenous Data Sovereignty in Australia: A Five‐Phase Framework for Indigenous Data Governance

items.abstract: <jats:p>Developing nations stand at the intersection of two historic forces: the relentless rise of autonomous artificial intelligence, and the continued global imbalance created by corruption, poor governance, and exploitative foreign investment. This paper proposes a unified, human-centric model for global development that blends AI safety, economic sovereignty, public-sector innovation, and educational revolution. The goal is not to slow technological evolution, but to give humanity-especially the poorest nations-the tools to rise with it.</jats:p>
title: Beyond Survival: A Unified Framework for AI Governance, Economic Sovereignty, and Human-Centric Development in Emerging Nations.

items.abstract: <jats:p>The European Commission has outlined a comprehensive vision, ambition and strategy for its data economy. The goal is to unlock Europe’s data potential for innovation and societal value, while safeguarding digital autonomy and data sovereignty. The Common European Data Spaces are developed as the means to do so. As the architectures, standards and building blocks are rapidly maturing, the main challenges for their large-scale deployment and adoption are shifting towards governance, business and innovation management. In this inaugural lecture, Harrie Bastiaansen presents his vision and research agenda to address these challenges. The goals are to improve value creation, to decrease complexity and to stimulate adoption of the overarching data sharing ecosystem. A combined community-driven and participant-driven approach for trusted and interoperable data sharing across sectors, borders and data spaces is presented as the means to do so.</jats:p>
title: Unlocking Europe’s Data Potential
subtitle: Digital Sovereignty, Innovation, and Governance in Times of Geopolitical Change

items.abstract: <jats:p>Deeply divided societies repeatedly fail under the centralized Westphalian model, which assigns sovereignty wholesale to one capital before any shared function can operate. This paper advances a conditional hypothesis: where parties are materially interdependent, at least one will not yet settle ultimate territorial status, and a minimal guarantor capacity exists, legally protected functional institutions can improve service continuity without agreement on status. It introduces the Universal Framework for Divided Sovereignty (UFDS), which unbundles sovereignty into five functional pillars (identity charters, property and infrastructure boards, municipal security units, algorithmic fiscal clearing, and shared-site administration) and entrenches them under a status non-prejudice clause. The claimed contribution is integration, not invention. Each component has precedent; UFDS combines them around a distinct sequencing principle, function before status, with an explicit legal architecture, adversarial failure protocols, and falsifiable hypotheses. The paper compares UFDS with federal, confederal, consociational, autonomy, and joint-management arrangements and identifies the narrow problem for which each is insufficient. It specifies the legal instruments and the constitutional questions they raise, models six forms of strategic abuse and the framework's behaviour when safeguards fail, and proposes indicators, comparators, and simulation designs, while stating that simulation cannot establish how real actors will behave. Applications to Kashmir and Israel-Palestine, Lebanon, and Nigeria show where the proposition is most and least plausible.</jats:p>
title: Polycentric Governance and Non-Territorial Sovereignty:&nbsp;A Functional Framework for Divided and Post-conflict States

<jats:p>Abstract:
This academic monograph develops a comprehensive framework for Quantum-AI legal intelligence across regulatory compliance, data sovereignty and algorithmic governance. It argues that contemporary legal systems increasingly confront decision environments shaped by automated models, platform infrastructures, cross-border data flows, post-quantum security risks and institutional demands for transparency. The manuscript conceptualises Quantum-AI not as a replacement for law, legal reasoning or public accountability, but as an advanced decision-support layer for optimization, uncertainty modelling, secure computation, evidentiary traceability and governance-aware analytics. Across five chapters, the book progresses from foundations and research design to causal explanation, trustworthy machine learning, sovereign data infrastructure and sectoral policy impact. It introduces conceptual diagrams, analytical tables, mathematical framing, evaluation metrics, risk frameworks and operational protocols that can guide researchers, regulators, legal technologists and policymakers. Global applicability is emphasised across South Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas, with attention to public administration, regulated industries, data protection, digital public infrastructure and institutional readiness. The central contribution is a doctoral-level architecture for designing legal intelligence systems that are accurate, explainable, contestable, sovereignty-aware and resilient in the quantum era.

items.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter addresses the challenges of datafication of finance and financial data sovereignty. Section II considers the datafication of finance. Section III considers the intersection of data, finance, and data governance, highlighting emerging general data governance styles. Section IV highlights the intersection of financial data regulation and personal data regulation in the context of the evolution of a range of Open Banking strategies focusing on personal financial data. Section V presents four emerging financial data governance strategies, exemplified by the United States, EU, China, and India, seeking to bring together finance and its regulation with their evolving domestic data governance regimes. Section VI elaborates on how the result of differences in these strategies combined with prudential objectives converges toward territorialization via data localization. Section VII addresses this growing challenge of fragmentation by outlining how the well-developed transnational regulatory frameworks in finance offer an opportunity to develop technological solutions and approaches that may, in fact, support both the objectives of financial and data regulation.</jats:p>
title: The Emergence of Financial Data Governance and the Challenge of Financial Data Sovereignty

items.abstract: <jats:p>As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes value-laden societal outcomes worldwide, the imperative for robust governance has become critical. Yet the global AI governance literature remains disproportionately Western-centric, frequently overlooking the structural and infrastructural realities of Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). This paper bridges the gap between theoretical critique and practical implementation by proposing a Five-Pillar AI Governance Framework tailored to SSA. The framework is substantiated through a qualitative documentary analysis of contemporary African policy developments, employing a most-different systems comparative design across the divergent regulatory pathways of Rwanda, Nigeria, and the African Union. Policy evidence is extracted and coded against three governance indicators - infrastructural sovereignty, stakeholder participation, and institutional enforcement - and mapped onto the proposed structural pillars to produce an operational governance matrix. The resulting architectural blueprint offers African policymakers a practical roadmap for harnessing AI safely while safeguarding local digital sovereignty.</jats:p>
title: Decolonizing Digital Sovereignty: An Operational Framework and Policy Analysis of AI Governance in&nbsp;Sub-Saharan Africa

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The term
                    <jats:italic>data sovereignty</jats:italic>
                    —the principle that data is subject to the laws and governance of the country where it is collected or stored—faces implementation challenges. The legal deadlock over how to regulate transatlantic (E.U.–U.S.) data transfers reveal the difficulties of asserting “sovereignty” over data, a resource that flows transnationally through digital technologies. Among global regulatory efforts, the European Union’s struggle to ensure the supremacy of its data protection and privacy laws represents an interesting case from which to derive new theoretical and conceptual insights. This paper advances
                    <jats:italic>data agency</jats:italic>
                    —as agency mediated
                    <jats:italic>by</jats:italic>
                    data, not
                    <jats:italic>over</jats:italic>
                    it. The intention is to advance a term that moves beyond the limits of data sovereignty to explain how governance over data-driven systems is distributed and contested. The manuscript suggests pragmatic pathways for more effective governance as mere “control” over data is not enough to achieve meaningful insights derived from data technologies.
                  </jats:p>
title: Advancing data agency: A conceptual framework to support data sovereignty

items.abstract: <jats:p>The telecommunications industry is undergoing a paradigm shift toward open, disaggregated, and automated networks, necessitating a secure, regulated, and sovereign approach to telemetry data sharing among stakeholders. This paper introduces a pioneering governance framework that leverages the Eclipse Dataspace Components Connector to enforce policy-driven telemetry data exchange within the multi-stakeholder telco ecosystem. The proposed framework offers advanced anonymization mechanisms and dynamic policy-enforcement controls, including stakeholder-specific, time-based, and location-aware access restrictions, ensuring compliance with privacy regulations. In this regard, we propose two novel, to our knowledge, data model vocabularies for modeling the telemetry data sharing problem according to the principles of the International Data Spaces Association, enabling seamless integration and valid application of data sovereignty principles. We experimentally validate the proposed framework through four use-cases designed based on real-world scenarios from operational settings, which address various stakeholder-specific data exchange scenarios, over the Fraunhofer HHI’s software-defined-networking-enabled photonics testbed. We present the policy enforcement capabilities of the framework through various experiments. Additionally, we report an in-depth performance analysis to reveal the latency and communication overhead of the proposed framework compared to conventional telemetry sharing solutions that do not comply with data sovereignty principles. The work in this paper demonstrates innovative contributions that enable data governance within optical networks, driving forward compliance, innovation, and stakeholder collaboration.</jats:p>
title: Network data sharing: a governance framework for ensuring data sovereignty and privacy compliance

items.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the shifting landscape of African cyber-jurisprudence, moving from the Malabo Convention (AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection) to the complex integration of the 2026 UN Convention Against Cybercrime. The central argument is that Africa faces a “double-edged fragmentation”: the external friction between global geopolitical blocs and the internal lack of harmonization between African states. This chapter provides an ecosystem-level analysis of African cross-border cooperation, focusing on the transition from colonial-era Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) to modern, intelligence-led judicial cooperation. It further examines how jurisdictional fragmentation, mobile money ecosystems, and evidentiary challenges enable transnational cybercrime. The chapter concludes by assessing emerging threats posed by artificial intelligence and quantum computing, emphasizing the need for harmonized legal systems, institutional resilience, and collaborative governance to secure Africa's digital future.</jats:p>
title: African Digital Sovereignty, Cross-Border Cybercrime, and the Future of Networked Governance

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter seeks to address the challenges of datafication of finance and financial data sovereignty. Section II considers the datafication of finance. Section III considers the intersection of data, finance, and data governance, highlighting emerging general data governance styles. Section IV highlights the intersection of financial data regulation and personal data regulation, in the context of the evolution of a range of Open Banking strategies, focusing on personal financial data. Section V presents four emerging financial data governance strategies, exemplified by the United States, EU, China, and India, seeking to bring together finance and its regulation with their evolving domestic data governance regimes. Section VI elaborates how the result of differences in these strategies combined with prudential objectives are converging toward territorialization via data localization. Section VII addresses this growing challenge of fragmentation by outlining how the well-developed transnational regulatory frameworks in finance offer an opportunity to develop technological solutions and approaches that may in fact support both the objectives of financial and data regulation.</jats:p>
title: The Emergence of Financial Data Governance and the Challenge of Financial Data Sovereignty

items.abstract: <jats:p>International organizations have struggled to establish binding rules on cross-border data flows despite the growing importance of trade in digitally delivered services (DDS). This paper argues that cooperation is difficult because governments pursue data sovereignty through different instruments for asserting authority over data. We distinguish strict localization measures, which keep data, processing, or infrastructure under domestic jurisdiction, from conditional flow regimes, which permit transfers when firms or destination jurisdictions satisfy domestic legal requirements. We develop a theory in which DDS competitiveness raises the costs of territorial control, while political accountability shapes whether firm opposition and consumer privacy concerns influence policy. Using new data on cross-border data restrictions for more than 150 countries from 2005 to 2024, we show that data sovereignty measures differ from conventional goods trade protection. Leveraging exogenous variation in topographic constraints on DDS competitiveness, we find that revealed comparative advantage in DDS is associated with fewer strict localization measures, especially in higher-accountability systems. IOs struggle to govern data flows because domestic political environments lead governments to assert authority through different forms of data sovereignty. * Tomás Rogaler and Simón González Ugarte provided excellent research assistance. The comments of Robert Basedow and participants at DIESL workshop at Oxford University and KCL's junior IPE scholar workshop, are especially acknowledged.</jats:p>
title: Data Sovereignty: Firms, Accountability, and the Challenge of International Governance

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid growth of stablecoins is reshaping digital finance by transforming payment systems, cross-border transactions, and monetary governance while creating new challenges for monetary sovereignty and financial stability. This chapter presents a conceptual analysis of how stablecoins influence monetary policy, regulatory governance, and the strategic role of Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs). Using an integrative review of academic and policy literature, it develops the Integrated Monetary Sovereignty Governance Framework (IMSGF), which explains the relationships among stablecoin adoption, payment system transformation, financial stability, regulatory governance, CBDC integration, public trust, and monetary sovereignty. The chapter proposes five conceptual propositions to support future empirical research. It concludes that adaptive regulation, international cooperation, interoperable CBDCs, and technology-enabled supervision are essential for balancing financial innovation with long-term monetary stability and institutional resilience.</jats:p>
title: An Integrated Governance Framework for Stablecoins and Monetary Sovereignty in the Digital Era

items.abstract: <jats:p>The accelerating global transition toward low-carbon energy systems has transformed critical minerals into strategic assets at the center of economic competitiveness, technological innovation, and geopolitical rivalry. As the world's leading producer of cobalt and one of the most mineral-endowed countries globally, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) occupies a pivotal position in emerging global value chains for electric mobility, renewable energy, battery technologies, and digital industries. Yet despite this extraordinary resource wealth, the country continues to experience persistent underdevelopment, institutional fragility, environmental degradation, and limited industrial transformation. Existing theoretical perspectives—including the resource curse, dependency theory, neo-extractivism, and global value chain analysis—provide important explanations for these outcomes but remain insufficient for conceptualizing pathways through which mineral abundance can be transformed into long-term innovation capacity and national prosperity. Building upon the emerging field of Innovationology, previously developed by Pitshou Moleka as a transdisciplinary science of innovation systems, adaptive intelligence, and societal transformation, this article proposes an Innovationological Framework for Critical Mineral Governance centered on the concept of innovation sovereignty. Innovation sovereignty is defined as the capacity of a nation to create, govern, retain, and continuously expand scientific, technological, industrial, institutional, and cognitive capabilities derived from its strategic resources. Rather than treating mining as an isolated extractive sector, the proposed framework conceptualizes critical minerals as catalysts for knowledge production, industrial learning, institutional adaptation, technological upgrading, and ecosystem-wide value creation. Drawing upon complexity science, systems thinking, innovation studies, adaptive governance, and sustainability transition scholarship, the article develops an integrated theoretical model explaining the transition from extractive dependence toward innovation-driven development. Although the Democratic Republic of Congo serves as the principal analytical case, the framework offers broader implications for mineral-rich economies seeking to reposition themselves within the rapidly evolving global green economy. The study contributes to innovation theory, natural resource governance, and African development by advancing innovation sovereignty as a new paradigm for governing critical minerals in the twenty-first century.</jats:p>
title: From Extractivism to Innovation Sovereignty : An Innovationological Framework for Critical Mineral Governance in the Democratic Republic of Congo
